content: For global guidelines on managing sexually transmitted infections (STIs) to be effective, they must address both settings with limited access to modern technologies and those where such technologies are available. Countries are strongly encouraged to incorporate updated global guidance into their national protocols, tailoring these recommendations to their local epidemiological data and patterns of antimicrobial resistance. National guidelines for STI management should be developed in close collaboration with local experts in STIs, public health, and laboratory sciences. Phase 1 focuses on treatment recommendations for specific STIs, including Chlamydia trachomatis (chlamydia), Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonorrhea), HSV-2 (genital herpes), and Treponema pallidum (syphilis), as well as syphilis screening and treatment in pregnant women. This phase also includes the development of syndromic management guidelines and clinical management packages. Phase 2 emphasizes STI prevention strategies, such as condom use, behavior change communication, biomedical interventions, and vaccines. Phases 1 and 2 will later be consolidated into a single comprehensive document. Phase 3 will address the treatment of additional infections, including Trichomonas vaginalis (trichomoniasis), bacterial vaginosis, Candida albicans (candidiasis), Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid), Klebsiella granulomatis (donovanosis), human papillomavirus (HPV; genital warts/cervical cancer), Sarcoptes scabiei (scabies), and Pthirus pubis (pubic lice). Phase 4 will focus on laboratory diagnosis and screening for STIs. Gonorrhea, caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, is the second most common bacterial STI globally, with significant health and economic burdens. In 2012, WHO estimated 78 million new cases among individuals aged 15–49 years, with the highest prevalence in the Western Pacific and African regions. Co-infection with Chlamydia trachomatis occurs in 10–40% of gonorrhea cases. In men, gonorrhea typically presents as urethritis with symptoms such as urethral discharge and dysuria, while in women, it is often asymptomatic or associated with non-specific symptoms like abnormal vaginal discharge, dysuria, and lower abdominal discomfort. Untreated infections can lead to severe complications, including pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, and ectopic pregnancy in women, and epididymitis and infertility in men. Neonates born to infected mothers may develop neonatal conjunctivitis, which, if untreated, can result in blindness. Laboratory diagnosis of N. gonorrhoeae can be achieved through culture, nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), or Gram stain. NAATs are highly sensitive and specific, suitable for various sample types, including urine, vaginal, cervical, and urethral swabs. However, NAATs cannot provide antimicrobial susceptibility data, making culture an essential parallel diagnostic method for susceptibility testing. In resource-limited settings, Gram stains may offer a cost-effective alternative for symptomatic men, though they are less reliable for asymptomatic infections and other sample types. The emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in N. gonorrhoeae has necessitated updates to treatment guidelines. Resistance to many antibiotics, including quinolones and third-generation cephalosporins, has been reported globally, raising concerns about untreatable infections. The WHO guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations for treating gonorrhea and support countries in updating their national guidelines. These guidelines are intended for healthcare providers at all levels, as well as policymakers and program managers involved in STI management. The guideline development process involved systematic reviews of evidence, prioritization of key clinical questions, and input from international STI experts. Recommendations were formulated based on the GRADE approach, considering the benefits and risks of interventions, patient values, resource use, and feasibility. Strong recommendations are indicated by the phrase The WHO STI guideline recommends, while conditional recommendations use The WHO STI guideline suggests. Dissemination of the guidelines will occur through printed publications, online platforms, and major conferences, with support provided to countries for adaptation and implementation. Feedback from end-users will be collected to identify barriers to implementation and areas for improvement. Countries are encouraged to conduct local studies to adapt the guidelines to their specific STI epidemiology and AMR patterns. In the absence of local data, the global recommendations can be adopted as presented.
